newsitem.title: FRANCE: Students, doctors protests at French government.
newsitem.headline: Students, doctors protests at French government.

text.p: Students and teachers marched in Paris to demand more aid for education on Sunday and striking doctors protested against health curbs in twin challenges to France's centre-right government.

"All together", "Against economic horror" the students, parents and teachers chanted as they marched through the capital in a carnival atmosphere to the music of bands and carrying banners and balloons.
Police estimated 15,000 people took part in the protest for more resources for education and youth employment. Organisers said the turnout was 70,000.

About one in four people in France aged under 25 is without a job, double the national average, despite President Jacques Chirac's pledges of a war for jobs when he came to power in 1995. "Promises to win power -- we're waiting!" banners said.

In a separate sign of discontent, thousands of junior hospital doctors on strike since March 11 marched through Paris and other French cities dressed in white coats to denounce curbs on health spending.
Police estimated 2,500 people marched in Paris, doctors said at least 10,000 took part. "I'm daft, I voted Chirac", one banner said.

Prime Minister Alain Juppe says that sweeping health care reforms, the main trigger of a crippling 24-day wave of strikes in late 1995, are vital partly to enable France to qualify for a planned single European currency from 1999.
The doctors, who marched in other cities including Lyon and Grenoble, say spending curbs will mean a rationing of France's universal health care.
The stoppage has cut services at 16 of France's 26 teaching hospitals, but emergency care is assured. Doctors also say their pay does not match their gruelling hours.
In Marseille, doctors scaled the chimney of a crematorium on Saturday to unfurl a giant banner proclaiming "strike".
Public health care spending is the leading factor in France's welfare deficit, expected to show a shortfall of about 33 billion francs ($5.8 billion) in 1997 after 51.6 billion last year.
Labour Minister Jacques Barrot said the government would stand firm after making concessions to doctors last week.
"If we give up here or there, on some of these issues, then opponents of the reform will be inclined to see the whole thing disappear," he told the weekly Journal du Dimanche.
Of the students' demands, Barrot said: "The president is responding to the expectations of the young...He wants a more dynamic France where the young find their place."

Two weeks ago, Chirac called for a drive to equip all French secondary schools with computers by the year 2000 and to eradicate illiteracy as part of a drive to bolster education and youth employment.
